flashcards.q: What older tools did uv consolidate, and what's its defining property?
flashcards.a: Replaces pip + virtualenv/venv + pyenv + poetry/pipenv with one Rust binary managing dependency resolution, venv creation, interpreter installation, and lockfiles. Defining property: raw speed (~100ms installs vs pip's ~30s for equivalent resolution).

flashcards.q: What older tools did ruff consolidate, and why does its speed matter beyond convenience?
flashcards.a: Replaces flake8(+plugins) + isort + pyupgrade + largely black (via ruff format). ~200ms for 100k LOC makes running the FULL rule set on every save/commit practical -- this causally enabled teams to enforce stricter linting than the old slower stack allowed.

flashcards.q: Why does mypy --strict adoption normally need to be incremental rather than a flag-day switch?
flashcards.a: Strict mode bundles many checks (no untyped defs, no implicit Any) that all require genuinely complete type coverage to pass cleanly -- a single untyped function or unstubbed third-party dependency can cascade into hundreds of errors on an existing partially-typed codebase, which teams routinely abandon. Per-module overrides in pyproject.toml let strictness expand incrementally.

flashcards.q: What problem does a lockfile (uv.lock) solve that a loose requirements.txt does not?
flashcards.a: A requirements.txt without pinned transitive dependencies can resolve to different actual versions at different times/machines, causing 'works on my machine' bugs. A lockfile pins the exact resolved version of every dependency (direct and transitive), guaranteeing identical installs until deliberately regenerated.

flashcards.q: Why should a full test suite generally NOT go in a pre-commit hook?
flashcards.a: Pre-commit hooks block every commit synchronously -- once commits become slow, developers predictably start using --no-verify, which silently skips ALL hooks, not just the slow one. Keep pre-commit to fast checks (linting/formatting); reserve slow checks (full test suite) for CI.

flashcards.q: Distinguish a build backend from a dependency management tool.
flashcards.a: Build backend (hatchling/setuptools/flit-core, in [build-system]) actually produces a wheel/sdist per PEP 517. Dependency manager (uv/poetry) resolves/installs/locks dependencies and delegates actual building to whichever backend is configured -- these are independent, composable choices; switching one doesn't require switching the other.

flashcards.q: Why did pyproject.toml replace setup.py as the metadata source?
flashcards.a: setup.py is executable Python code -- discovering metadata required actually running arbitrary code (slow, unsafe, environment-dependent). pyproject.toml is a single, purely declarative static TOML file every tool can read without executing anything.

flashcards.q: Why might a team choose pyright or ty over mypy, and is it purely a speed decision?
flashcards.a: Both offer substantially faster check times than mypy's pure-Python implementation, valuable for very large codebases. Not purely speed -- different checkers have historically had subtly different interpretations of edge-case typing scenarios, so switching carries real migration/re-triage risk, not just a drop-in upgrade.
